 Analysis 
 Pune Weather Breaks Records as October Turns Exceptionally Dry
 By Maria Dsouza 
 November 1, 2026 
 0 
 Copy URL Facebook Linkedin X WhatsApp 
 Pune weather produced a sharp break from recent October patterns in 2026, with the India Meteorological Department’s Shivajinagar station recording only 1.7 mm of rain for the month while the average maximum temperature reached 34.66 degrees Celsius. The combination made October not merely dry, but unusually hot by the city’s recent record.
 The significance of the month lies in the contrast between what Pune normally experiences after the southwest monsoon and what happened this year. October is generally a transition period: the monsoon withdraws, but localised thunderstorms can still bring rain across the city and surrounding districts. In 2026, that transition was unusually abrupt. The southwest monsoon withdrew from Pune on October 3, around a week earlier than the city’s normal withdrawal date of about October 10. The thunderstorms that often follow the monsoon were also absent.
 The result was a month that stood out both for its lack of rain and for its heat. According to data cited in the Indian Express report, the average maximum temperature in Shivajinagar was 34.66 degrees Celsius in October 2026. The average maximum in October 2025 was 31.3 degrees Celsius, while the highest average maximum since 2014 had previously been 33.2 degrees Celsius, recorded in 2018.
 The rainfall figures show an equally clear departure. Shivajinagar received 1.7 mm in October 2026, the lowest October total since 2014. In recent years, October rainfall at the station ranged from 18.6 mm in 2023 to 61.2 mm in 2024 and 67.3 mm in 2025. The contrast is even larger with October 2020, when the station recorded 313 mm, and October 2019, when it recorded 235 mm.
 That long variation is important because it shows why a monthly average alone cannot describe Pune’s post-monsoon weather. October rainfall has not followed a stable pattern in the years cited. The same month has produced very wet conditions in some years and almost no rain in another. For a growing city, that variability complicates how seasonal conditions are interpreted by residents, administrators and infrastructure managers.
 The rainfall recorded across Pune district on October 31 also shows that the dry conditions were not uniform everywhere. Bhor received 67 mm over 24 hours, Shirur recorded 45.5 mm, Magarpatta received 18 mm, Nimgiri recorded 17 mm and Pashan received 7 mm. The Shivajinagar rain gauges remained dry. These figures do not describe a single district-wide weather experience; they show how sharply rainfall can vary between locations over a short distance.
 That variation is a central part of the urban weather challenge. A city may be described as dry using data from one principal station while individual neighbourhoods or nearby parts of the district receive measurable rainfall. The distinction matters for interpreting local water conditions, stormwater performance and weather alerts, although the supplied data does not establish how Pune’s water systems or urban services responded during the month.
 The atmospheric explanation offered in the report points to several overlapping factors rather than one simple cause. The first was the early withdrawal of the southwest monsoon. Once the monsoon moved away earlier than usual, Pune lost a major source of seasonal moisture at the start of the month.
 The second was the absence of the thunderstorms that commonly bring rain to Pune during the post-monsoon period. From the middle of September, these storms can be triggered by weather systems developing over the Bay of Bengal or by discontinuities in wind patterns along the west coast and across Marathwada and Madhya Maharashtra. In 2026, the weather systems required to generate that activity did not become strong enough, according to the expert cited in the report.
 A third factor was the early formation of an anticyclone, or high-pressure system, generally associated with Gujarat after the middle of October. Its influence kept Maharashtra under predominantly dry conditions and limited cloud cover. Less cloud cover also helped create conditions for higher daytime temperatures, linking the month’s rainfall deficit with its unusual heat.
 Moisture movement from the Bay of Bengal was another missing element. Although the Northeast Monsoon established itself over Tamil Nadu, the easterly trough that normally transports moisture inland did not extend far enough north to benefit Maharashtra. At the same time, no significant low-pressure system developed over the Arabian Sea to carry moisture towards Madhya Maharashtra and Marathwada.
 This explanation also challenges an easy attribution to El Nino. The expert cautioned against treating El Nino as the direct reason for Pune’s dry October, pointing to 2015 as a counterexample. That year was also associated with El Nino, yet Shivajinagar received 76.7 mm of rain in October. The preceding September had recorded 173 mm, compared with 64.1 mm in September 2026. The comparison suggests that the conditions immediately before October, as well as the availability and direction of moisture during the month, are important to understanding the outcome.
 The institutional lesson is that Pune’s seasonal weather cannot be explained through a single national climate label. The local outcome depended on the timing of monsoon withdrawal, the formation or absence of thunderstorms, high-pressure conditions and the failure of moisture-bearing systems to reach Maharashtra. These are separate atmospheric processes that combined to produce one dry and hot month.
 For urban governance, the data also underlines the importance of reading weather at more than one scale. Shivajinagar remains the primary IMD station for Pune, making its long-term record valuable for comparisons. But the October 31 figures from Bhor, Shirur, Magarpatta, Nimgiri and Pashan demonstrate that district and neighbourhood-level observations can tell a different story on the same day. Planning decisions based only on a central station may miss the uneven distribution of rainfall across the wider urban region.
 The evidence does not establish whether the October pattern will continue into the coming months. The IMD forecast issued on October 31 said above-normal maximum and minimum temperatures were likely over most parts of the country in November 2026. That forecast provides an immediate reason to monitor temperatures, but it does not by itself determine Pune’s rainfall performance or establish a long-term trend.
 What October confirms is narrower but significant: Pune experienced its lowest October rainfall at Shivajinagar since 2014 alongside its highest average maximum temperature for October in the period cited. The causes identified in the supplied report are connected to monsoon timing, local thunderstorm activity, high-pressure conditions and weakened moisture transport. The larger urban question is how Pune’s institutions interpret and manage weather when the city’s principal station, its neighbourhoods and the wider district do not experience the same conditions. November’s temperature and rainfall observations will show whether October was an isolated departure or part of a broader seasonal shift.
